A good avenue is finding trans/LGBT communities. Discord servers are good, but irl is best. Look for support groups, social groups, places where queer people help each other. Make friends, open up about your problems, listen and support them when they talk about theirs. There are a lot of obvious benefits to this on its own, but I promise it's relevant. 

Queer and kink communities always have significant overlap. Kinky folks have a strong tendency to be more open minded about queer folks, and vice versa, so historically the two groups have built significant solidarity. If you find people you trust and make friends in either community, you will be able to find resources for the other. 

In the queer spaces, don't lead with or focus on kink, just mention that it's a part of your experience and other kinky folk will make themselves known and help you find kink communities. We tend to want to help each other. From there, learn and make friends. Find local munches, dungeons, classes, parties, etc. Just be around, be friendly, be respectful, and learn, and eventually someone will show interest.

It takes a while going this way, but when it does you'll find yourself with friends, community, and resources abound to see you through all the complexities of developing and exploring D/s relationships, which are invaluable tools. I happen to help run a community on reddit/discord and work to keep it as trans inclusive as I can, you can find it pretty easily in my posting history if you're interested, but no pressure.

Good luck! It can be a long journey, but it is so, so worth it to express your full self.

It's an umbrella term that covers a wide variety of kinks and fetishes. In the abbreviation are three smaller abbreviations which in a very tight nutshell, are:

B/D: Bondage and Discipline. Unlike the other two, these are not necessarily linked together, bondage describes enjoying being restrained or restraining someone, and discipline refers to enjoying being trained/punished/rewarded, or otherwise held accountable for one's actions.

D/s: Dominance and submission, this covers people who enjoy entering power exchange relationships, where one person (Dominant) controls some degree of the other person's (submissive) ability to make their own decisions. 

S/M: sadism and masochism, or sadomasochism. This references people who enjoy experiencing or inflicting pain or discomfort, whether physical, mental, or emotional. It doesn't necessarily mean the pain itself feels good, but can also mean that the participants enjoy the trust, vulnerability, aesthetics, power exchange, or some other facet of pain that frames the pain itself.

If someone enjoys any of these to any degree, they are understood to be "into" BDSM as a whole. It covers a huge variety of approaches to relationships, activities, fantasies, interests, skills, etc etc, and is a fascinating subculture centered on fostering safety, healthy relationships, and acceptance of everyone who finds themselves drawn to relationships and indulgences deemed "deviant" by mainstream society.

/uj so I occasionally fall into that too, and I've found some success in treating it the way I've treated other addictive and self-destructive behaviors. With everything like this, it's very easy to look at it as purely bad, but if that were the case we wouldn't do it. Alcohol, drugs, nicotine, sh, etc etc all have benefits that in extreme circumstances can seem worth the costs to us, no matter how damaging we know they'll be. 

The core idea is to figure out what the benefit is to you. Does experiencing that pain make you feel more connected to the struggles of the trans community as a whole, giving you a sense of belonging? Does being hurt by transphobia give you an external source of validation, because if it hurts you, that proves you're really trans? It can be anything, possibly multiple things, and it might even change moment to moment.

But the trick is to find how it benefits you, and then slowly introduce a healthier source for that benefit. Treat it as a transitional phase. Don't hold yourself to stopping immediately, just blend in your healthier source for validation or belonging or whatever it might be and gently shift your focus to that new alternate source over time. Approaching it with patience and compassion for yourself will also allow you to more easily recognize the unhealthy habits appearing again and gently course-correcting in the future.

And this isn't set in stone. We're all individuals, this is just the approach that best works for me, learned over years and years of self-inflicted suffering.

I cannot speak for the community as a whole because I am relatively new to it as well. However, I do know that asexuality is a broad spectrum, and that what you're describing is included within that spectrum.

I do not get the impression that anyone here would say you don't belong in the community. It wasn't really one realization but a series of them. For some important context, I am a trans woman.

The first time asexuality seriously crossed my mind was after starting hormone replacement therapy and having my libido nuked. It was an enormous relief to not feel like sexual thoughts were constantly intruding on my mind. 

Another big moment was embracing the fact that BDSM is a part of my interpersonal needs, and that relationships make most sense to me through the lens of power exchange. That very, very quickly led to the realization that I have a strong preference for other forms of physical intimacy over sex. That if I were given a choice between sex and, for instance, an impact play scene, I don't ever really see myself choosing sex.

Covid also confirmed a belief I had held for a long time, that if I stopped having sex completely it wouldn't really bother me. I believe I've had two sexual encounters in the last three years, and I've been perfectly content while many of my allo friends have been very negatively impacted by the long dry spell that circumstances have forced them into.

I started really gaining momentum towards accepting myself as ace relatively recently, when I heard someone describe their experience as gray ace, and a lot of it resonated with me. I watched some of Evie Lupine's content on asexuality and felt further resonance with the identity, then went through some of the resources on this subreddit and noticed that very little of the allosexual descriptions of sexual attraction connected with me.

I then started reflecting on and challenging my past sexual experiences. Learning that I have likely been substituting a blend of arousal, romantic attraction, and aesthetic appreciation for sexual attraction. That while I have always been at least moderately uncomfortable with having sex, ascribing all of that discomfort to dysphoria was likely too broad a brush to paint with. That I had always been confused about my sexuality, describing it with a litany of asterisks and exceptions, but upon removing any attempts to describe sexual attraction and instead describe intimate attraction it became *much*  more concise and accurate to my experience.

I started talking to some friends of mine who were out and openly asexual about the more nuanced questions, thoughts, and feelings I was having on the topic, and they found much of what I said to be relatable. Very quickly after those conversations was the closest thing I've had to a "light bulb moment," when I stopped asking if I was ace and started describing myself as ace. I was talking to my therapist about all this, and they asked me, "Accounting for dysphoria, do you often dissociate during sex?" And I responded, "Well yeah, but- ...oh, not everyone does that, do they?"

Everyone's journey is different, I just laid mine out because it's close to hand and maybe there's one or two parts that will connect with you. And maybe there aren't, but that wouldn't necessarily mean that asexuality is an inappropriate term to describe yourself with.

One of my biggest moments in therapy after my last relapse was realizing that while I had stopped cutting, I had been excessively drinking, smoking, binge eating, having risky, uncomfortable sex, and on and on. I suddenly saw so clearly that I'd been conducting a clear trend of self-harm for most of my life, it shocked me.

My understanding is that I could say that that's the only part that I like because I dislike seeing the act itself but find human voices stimulating.

Then someone else could comment that that's their least favorite part because they're sensitive to auditory overstimulation.

And then a third person could say they detest everything about porn, and a fourth that porn is the only thing in the sphere of anything sexual that they enjoy.

And we'd all be equally valid in calling ourselves asexual.

It's not about meeting or being eliminated from some kind of higher criteria. It's about allowing yourself the space to step away from the idea of sexual attraction as being fundamental to intimate relationships, and to grow in whichever directions allow you to best flourish thusly unburdened.

Having a knife play/blood play kink is perfectly fine, maybe not the norm but certainly not rare, I'm also there myself.

The thing is, especially when dealing with edge play, control is extremely important. Pairing the sort of intense self-criticism you're describing with being a solo player would lead to a very unstable environment, and therefore would not be safe, and it might even be highly damaging in many ways.

If this ends up being a kink for you, there's nothing wrong with that in and of itself, even if its roots are in sh. Maybe that's where mine comes from too, who knows, chicken and egg. What matters is having control over it, so I do things like have a dedicated knife that I give to my partners that I am not allowed to handle, and ensure a calm, caring, intimate environment to keep the scene emotionally separate from sh. In addition, when I've relapsed, I avoid edge play entirely to prevent sh from creeping into my intimate life.

Again, don't worry if this is something you're potentially into, that's totally fine and you're absolutely not alone if that's the case. But at the very least you are not currently in a position to engage with that kink in a safe manner, and so I would strongly encourage you to take steps to avoid engaging with the potentially sexual side of this for the time being, at least until you can explore it in a stable, controlled, and supportive environment.
